extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, instrument-makers, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing experimental reports and instrument descriptions in natural philosophy (magnetism, optics, meteorology, astronomy, comparative anatomy) with emphasis on measurement, reproducibility, and methodological transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on uncalibrated observational reports / note observer error
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place too much reliance on casual observational reports (e.g., pilots') because of gross errors and local disturbances that are not easy for them to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance: "too much reliance must not be laid upon the observations of pilots, by reason of the gross errors which it is not easy for them to avoid. For it often happens, that near the place where the compass is, there is much iron, which draws the needle, and causes it to show a point on the horizon much different from what it would, were it farther from the iron..." — therefore prefer controlled/instrumented observation over informal reports and explicitly account for local perturbing factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe instruments and constructions with precise dimensions and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete dimensions, materials, and construction details for instruments so others can reproduce or judge the device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from text: "I caused a ring of 3 inches diameter to be made of steel wire, from which issued three radii of very fine brass wire..."; burning speculum: "outer circle ... near 3½ ells in diameter... made of a copper plate scarcely twice as thick as the back of an ordinary knife... the focus is 2 ells off." Include such numeric and material detail in instrument reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document experimental procedure and testing protocol (including how devices are magnetized/touched)
rubrics_metrics.description: State exactly how an instrument or specimen was prepared and tested (e.g., method of magnetization, placement of filings, pointed-iron probes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "I gave the magnetical touch to this steel ring, by applying indifferently to a point of it one of the poles of a strong loadstone, and the other pole of the stone to the opposite point..."; describe test procedures (strewed filings on paper, presented pointed iron) so observations can be understood and reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and report controlled experimental conditions (temperature, counterbalancing, steady inputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep key variables constant and describe how they were held constant (thermometer, counterpoise, control of heat source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley's procedure: "we brought the water to the same degree of heat, which is observed to be that of the air in our hottest summers; the thermometer nicely showing it. This done, we affixed the pan of water... and exactly counterpoised it with weights... by the application or removal of the pan of coals, we found it very easy to maintain the water in the same degree of heat precisely." Report how stability was achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative measurements with units, conversions, and full calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report measured quantities, explicit units, conversions, and the arithmetic/assumptions used to scale results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley gives weights in grains and ounces, converts cubic feet to cubic inches, computes thickness evaporated and scales up to square degrees of sea: e.g. "the weight of 233 grains is... 35 parts out of 38 of a cubic inch... the area... 49 square inches... the thickness... the 53d part of an inch". Include such explicit numeric steps and any reference constants used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainties, make conservative assumptions, and state approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly note sources of uncertainty and, when appropriate, choose conservative/simple values for ease of calculation or to avoid overclaiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley: "but we will suppose it only the sixtieth part, for the facility of calculation." De la Hire: notes irregular stones cause irregularity. Also allow generous margins when estimating large-scale quantities (river flows, evaporation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use replication and independent verification (including institutional checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify experiments by repeating, by alternate constructions, and by independent examination (e.g., Royal Society examined its terrella).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "these experiments gave me the curiosity of making another..." and "it was ordered that the terrella... should be examined... and on trial it was found..." Encourage replication and institutional verification to settle disputes about effects or pole-translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and control for confounding factors (local iron, wind, salinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: List and where possible control factors that could confound results (local magnetic iron near a compass, winds accelerating surface evaporation, salt concentration of water used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: magnetism: iron near the compass distorts reading; evaporation: Halley salted the water "to the same degree as is the common sea-water" and notes winds can 'lick up' surface water faster than heat-induced evaporation. Explicitly report such controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support instrument performance claims with specific demonstrations and observed outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming instrument capabilities, demonstrate with timed/observed trials and specific effects on materials (melting times, burning through metal, boiling water).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burning speculum examples: "A piece of wood, put in the focus, flames in a moment... Water... presently boils... a plate of iron... is immediately seen to be red hot... a piece of tin or lead 3 inches thick... melts away in drops..." Provide concrete demonstrations and times where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate multi-location observations for astronomical events and report precise timings/measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe celestial events from multiple sites and record exact local times and quantitative measurements (chords, digits) to determine quantities like lunar parallax and latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solar eclipse section lists observations from London, Greenwich, Bridgetown, Nuremburg, Ulm, Leipsic, Breslaw, each reporting beginning/middle/end times and chord/digits. Use such coordinated data for geometric inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide comparative, detailed anatomical description and link morphology to function
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting dissections, describe organ form, relative sizes, and special structures, compare across species, and discuss functional implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural history entries describe epiglottis size in sea calf, oesophagus in cormorant, caecum differences, muscle for erecting quills, etc. Comparative notes (porcupine vs hedgehog) and functional interpretations are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite prior work and improve accessibility (translations, republication) when original copies are scarce
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge earlier publications, the provenance of materials, and provide translations or editions when the original is hard to obtain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoirs: translated because "the difficulty of procuring copies of the French edition... was no small inducement to this translation." Cite previous relevant publications and provenance (e.g., society's terrella gifted by King Charles II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale small experiments thoughtfully to large-scale inferences and state scaling assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When extrapolating from tabletop experiments to regional/global magnitudes (e.g., evaporation from a pan to the Mediterranean), state the scaling methodology and justify assumptions (day length, area estimates, river flow multipliers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley scales the pan result to "every 10 square inches yields in vapour per diem a cube inch... a square degree... the whole Mediterranean... 5280 millions of tons." He also admits difficulty and makes allowance choices (rivers 10 times Thames, area estimates). Document scaling steps and their caveats.
